He was poorer than other Cynics because he'd given up not just owning things but even asking for things. Yet they still accused him of not being needy enough — as if he claimed to be an expert on poverty, not virtue.

happy-life_section-19.originalText:
They say that Diodorus, the Epicurean philosopher, who within these last few days put an end to his life with his own hand, did not act according to the precepts of Epicurus, in cutting his throat: some choose to regard this act as the result of madness, others of recklessness; he, meanwhile, happy and filled with the consciousness of his own goodness, has borne testimony to himself by his manner of departing from life, has commended the repose of a life spent at anchor in a safe harbour, and has said what you do not like to hear, because you too ought to do it:

"I've lived, I've run the race which Fortune set me."
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: They say that Diodorus, an Epicurean philosopher, killed himself just a few days ago by cutting his throat. Critics claim this went against Epicurus's teachings. Some call it madness, others call it reckless. But Diodorus himself was happy and confident in his own goodness. The way he chose to die was his final testimony about himself. He praised the peace of a life lived safely in harbor, and said something you don't want to hear — because you should do the same thing: "I have lived. I have run the race that Fortune set for me."

happy-life_section-19.originalText: You argue about the life and death of another, and yelp at the name of men whom some peculiarly noble quality has rendered great, just as tiny curs do at the approach of strangers: for it is to your interest that no one should appear to be good, as if virtue in another were a reproach to all your crimes. You enviously compare the glories of others with your own dirty actions, and do not understand how greatly to your disadvantage it is to venture to do so: for if they who follow after virtue be greedy, lustful, and fond of power, what must you be, who hate the very name of virtue?
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: You argue about whether other people lived well or poorly. You bark at the names of men who became great through some noble quality — like small dogs yapping at strangers. It serves your purpose to make sure no one looks good, because if someone else is virtuous, it makes all your crimes look worse. You jealously compare other people's achievements to your own shameful actions. But you don't realize how badly this comparison makes you look. If even those who try to be virtuous still struggle with greed, lust, and power — what does that make you, someone who hates the very idea of virtue?

happy-life_section-19.originalText: You say that no one acts up to his professions, or lives according to the standard which he sets up in his discourses: what wonder, seeing that the words which they speak are brave, gigantic, and able to weather all the storms which wreck mankind, whereas they themselves are struggling to tear themselves away from crosses into which each one of you is driving his own nail. Yet men who are crucified hang from one single pole, but these who punish themselves are divided between as many crosses as they have lusts, but yet are given to evil speaking, and are so magnificent in their contempt of the vices of others that I should suppose that they had none of their own, were it not that some criminals when on the gibbet spit upon the spectators.
happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: You say no one lives up to what they preach or follows the high standards they set in their speeches. Is that really so surprising? Their words are bold and grand — strong enough to survive any storm that wrecks humanity. But they themselves are struggling to escape from crosses that they have built with their own hands, driving in every nail themselves. At least criminals on crosses hang from just one beam. But these people torture themselves on as many crosses as they have desires. And yet they still criticize others freely. They act so superior when condemning other people's vices that you'd think they had none of their own — except that even criminals hanging on the gallows sometimes spit on the people watching below.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
"Philosophers do not carry into effect all that they teach."
No; but they effect much good by their teaching, by the noble
thoughts which they conceive in their minds: would, indeed, that
they could act up to their talk: what could be happier than they
would be? but in the meanwhile you have no right to despise good
sayings and hearts full of good thoughts. Men deserve praise for
engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of
producing any results. Why need we wonder if those who begin to
climb a steep path do not succeed in ascending it very high? yet,
if you be a man, look with respect on those who attempt great things,
even though they fall. It is the act of a generous spirit to
proportion its efforts not to its own strength but to that of human
nature, to entertain lofty aims, and to conceive plans which are
too vast to be carried into execution even by those who are endowed
with gigantic intellects, who appoint for themselves the following
rules:
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish:
"Philosophers don't practice what they preach."

True enough. But they still do a lot of good through their teaching and the noble ideas they develop. I wish they could live up to their words completely — imagine how happy they would be! But you have no right to dismiss good advice and hearts full of good intentions just because of that.

People deserve credit for pursuing valuable studies, even if they don't achieve perfect results. Why should we be surprised when people who start climbing a steep mountain don't make it to the very top? Still, if you're human, show respect for those who attempt great things, even when they fail.

It takes a generous spirit to aim not just for what you can easily handle, but for what human nature itself can aspire to. To set lofty goals and make plans so grand that even people with enormous talents couldn't fully execute them. These are the people who set rules like this for themselves:

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
I will look upon death or upon a comedy with the same
expression of countenance: I will submit to labours, however great
they may be, supporting the strength of my body by that of
my mind: I will despise riches when I have them as much as when I
have them not; if they be elsewhere I will not be more gloomy, if
they sparkle around me I will not be more lively than I should
otherwise be: whether Fortune comes or goes I will take no notice
of her: I will view all lands as though they belong to me, and my
own as though they belonged to all mankind: I will so live as to
remember that I was born for others, and will thank Nature on this
account: for in what fashion could she have done better for me? she
has given me alone to all, and all to me alone. Whatever I may
possess, I will neither hoard it greedily nor squander it recklessly.
I will think that I have no possessions so real as those which I
have given away to deserving people: I will not reckon benefits by
their magnitude or number, or by anything except the value set upon
them by the receiver: I never will consider a gift to be a large
one if it be bestowed upon a worthy object. I will do nothing because
of public opinion, but everything because of conscience: whenever
I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the
Roman people are upon me while I do it.
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I will face death or a comedy with the same calm expression. I will take on any hard work, no matter how demanding, using my mind to strengthen my body. I will despise riches whether I have them or not. If I don't have money, I won't be gloomy. If wealth surrounds me, I won't be more excited than I should be. Whether Fortune comes or goes, I won't pay attention to her. I will see all lands as if they belong to me, and my own land as if it belongs to everyone. I will live remembering that I was born to serve others, and I will thank Nature for this. How could she have done better for me? She has given me alone to everyone, and everyone to me alone. Whatever I own, I won't hoard it greedily or waste it carelessly. I will think my only real possessions are what I have given to people who deserve them. I won't judge gifts by how big they are or how many I give, but only by how much the receiver values them. I will never think a gift is too large if it goes to someone worthy. I will do nothing for public opinion, but everything for my conscience. Whenever I act alone, I will imagine the eyes of the Roman people are watching me.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
In eating and drinking my
object shall be to quench the desires of Nature, not to fill and
empty my belly. I will be agreeable with my friends, gentle and
mild to my foes: I will grant pardon before I am asked for it, and
will meet the wishes of honourable men half way: I will bear in
mind that the world is my native city, that its governors are the
gods, and that they stand above and around me, criticizing whatever
I do or say. Whenever either Nature demands my breath again, or
reason bids me dismiss it, I will quit this life, calling all to
witness that I have loved a good conscience, and good pursuits;
that no one's freedom, my own least of all, has been impaired through
me." He who sets up these as the rules of his life will soar aloft
and strive to make his way to the gods: of a truth, even though he
fails, yet he

"Fails in a high emprise."[4]
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish:
When I eat and drink, I'll aim to satisfy my body's needs, not to stuff myself. I'll be kind to my friends and gentle even to my enemies. I'll forgive before anyone asks me to, and I'll meet good people halfway in their requests. I'll remember that the whole world is my home, that the gods rule it, and that they watch from above and all around me, judging everything I do and say. When nature calls for my last breath, or when reason tells me it's time to go, I'll leave this life. And I'll call everyone to witness that I loved having a clear conscience and noble goals, and that I never took away anyone's freedom — especially not my own.

Whoever lives by these rules will rise high and try to reach the gods. Even if he doesn't make it, at least he "fails in a high enterprise."

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
But you, who hate both virtue and those who practise it, do nothing
at which we need be surprised, for sickly lights cannot bear the
sun, nocturnal creatures avoid the brightness of day, and at its
first dawning become bewildered and all betake themselves to their
dens together: creatures that fear the light hide themselves in
crevices. So croak away, and exercise your miserable tongues in
reproaching good men: open wide your jaws, bite hard: you will break
many teeth before you make any impression.
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: But you, who hate virtue and anyone who tries to be good, are doing exactly what we'd expect. Sick eyes can't stand sunlight. Night creatures run from daylight and scramble back to their holes when dawn breaks. Animals that fear light hide in dark corners. So go ahead and croak your complaints. Use your pathetic tongues to attack good people. Open your mouths wide and bite as hard as you can — you'll break plenty of teeth before you leave even a scratch.

happy-life_section-21.originalText: "But how is it that this man studies philosophy and nevertheless lives the life of a rich man? Why does he say that wealth ought to be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible? Does he consider banishment to be an empty name, and say, "What evil is there in changing one country for another?" and yet, if permitted, does he not grow old in his native land? does he declare that there is no difference between a longer and a shorter time, and yet, if he be not prevented, lengthen out his life and flourish in a green old age?" His answer is, that these things ought to be despised, not that he should not possess them, but that he should not possess them with fear and trembling: he does not drive them away from him, but when they leave him he follows after them unconcernedly. Where, indeed, can fortune invest riches more securely than in a place from whence they can always be recovered without any squabble with their trustee?
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: But someone asks: "How can this man study philosophy and still live like a rich person? Why does he say wealth should be despised, yet keep his money? He says life should be despised, yet goes on living. He says health doesn't matter, yet takes careful care of his body and wants to stay as healthy as possible. He claims exile is meaningless and asks, 'What's so bad about changing countries?' Yet if he can help it, he grows old in his homeland. He says there's no difference between a long life and a short one, yet if nothing stops him, he tries to live as long as possible and enjoy a healthy old age." His answer is this: these things should be despised, but that doesn't mean you can't have them. It means you shouldn't cling to them in fear. He doesn't push them away, but when they leave him, he doesn't chase after them. Really, where could fortune put riches more safely than with someone who can always give them back without fighting their keeper?

happy-life_section-21.originalText: Marcus Cato, when he was praising Curius and Coruncanius and that century in which the possession of a few small silver coins were an offence which was punished by the Censor, himself owned four million sesterces; a less fortune no doubt, than that of Crassus, but larger than of Cato the Censor. If the amounts be compared, he had outstripped his great-grandfather further than he himself was outdone by Crassus, and if still greater riches had fallen to his lot, he would not have spurned them: for the wise man does not think himself unworthy of any chance presents: he does not love riches, but he prefers to have them; he does not receive them into his spirit, but only into his house: nor does he cast away from him what he already possesses, but keeps them, and is willing that his virtue should receive a larger subject-matter for its exercise.
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: Marcus Cato used to praise Curius and Coruncanius and their generation, when owning a few silver coins was seen as corruption that the Censor would punish. Yet Cato himself owned four million sesterces. This was less than Crassus had, but much more than his ancestor Cato the Censor ever owned. If you compare the numbers, Cato had outpaced his great-grandfather by more than Crassus had outpaced him. And if even greater wealth had come his way, he wouldn't have turned it down. A wise person doesn't think he's unworthy of good fortune. He doesn't love money, but he'd rather have it than not. He doesn't let wealth into his heart, just into his house. He doesn't throw away what he already has. Instead, he keeps it and uses it as raw material for practicing virtue on a larger scale.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Who can doubt, however, that the wise man, if he is rich, has a wider field for the development of his powers than if he is poor, seeing that in the latter case the only virtue which he can display is that of neither being perverted nor crushed by his poverty, whereas if he has riches, he will have a wide field for the exhibition of temperance, generosity, laboriousness, methodical arrangement, and grandeur. The wise man will not despise himself, however short of stature he may be, but nevertheless he will wish to be tall: even though he be feeble and one-eyed he may be in good health, yet he would prefer to have bodily strength, and that too, while he knows all the while that he has something which is even more powerful: he will endure illness, and will hope for good health: for some things, though they may be trifles compared with the sum total, and though they may be taken away without destroying the chief good, yet add somewhat to that constant cheerfulness which arises from virtue.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Who can doubt that a wise man has more room to show his wisdom when he's rich than when he's poor? When poor, he can only prove that poverty hasn't corrupted him or broken his spirit. But when rich, he has a wide field to display restraint, generosity, hard work, good planning, and nobility. A wise man won't hate himself for being short, but he'd still prefer to be tall. Even if he's weak and one-eyed but healthy, he'd rather have physical strength — knowing all the while that he has something far more powerful. He'll bear illness patiently but hope for good health. Some things may be small compared to what really matters. They can be taken away without destroying the chief good. But they do add something to that steady happiness that comes from virtue.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Riches encourage and brighten up such a man just as a sailor is delighted at a favourable wind that bears him on his way, or as people feel pleasure at a fine day or at a sunny spot in the cold weather. What wise man, I mean of our school, whose only good is virtue, can deny that even these matters which we call neither good nor bad have in themselves a certain value, and that some of them are preferable to others? to some of them we show a certain amount of respect, and to some a great deal. Do not, then, make any mistake: riches belong to the class of desirable things.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Wealth can cheer up and energize a wise person, just like a sailor feels joy when a good wind fills his sails, or like anyone enjoys a beautiful day or finding a warm, sunny spot when it's cold outside. What wise person from our school — who believes virtue is the only true good — would deny that these things we call 'neither good nor bad' still have some value? Some are clearly better than others. We give some things a little respect, and others quite a lot. So don't be confused: wealth belongs in the category of things worth wanting.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: "Why then," say you, "do you laugh at me, since you place them in the same position that I do?" Do you wish to know how different the position is in which we place them? If my riches leave me, they will carry away with them nothing except themselves: you will be bewildered and will seem to be left without yourself if they should pass away from you: with me riches occupy a certain place, but with you they occupy the highest place of all. In fine, my riches belong to me, you belong to your riches.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: "So why," you ask, "are you laughing at me when you value wealth just like I do?" Want to know the difference in how we see money? If I lose my wealth, it takes nothing with it except itself. But if you lose yours, you'll be lost and confused — like you've lost your very identity. For me, money has its place. For you, money is everything. In short: I own my wealth. Your wealth owns you.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty. The philosopher may own ample wealth, but will not own wealth that which has been torn from another, or which is stained with another's blood: his must be obtained without wronging any man, and without its being won by base means; it must be alike honourably come by and honourably spent, and must be such as spite alone could shake its head at. Raise it to whatever figure you please, it will still be an honourable possession, if, while it includes much which every man would like to call his own, there be nothing which any one can say is his own. Such a man will not forfeit his right to the favour of Fortune, and will neither boast of his inheritance nor blush for it if it was honourably acquired: yet he will have something to boast of, if he throw his house open, let all his countrymen come among his property, and say, "If any one recognizes here anything belonging to him, let him take it." What a great man, how excellently rich will he be, if after this speech he possesses as much as he had before! I say, then, that if he can safely and confidently submit his accounts to the scrutiny of the people, and no one can find in them any item upon which he can lay hands, such a man may boldly and unconcealedly enjoy his riches.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: Stop telling philosophers they can't have money. No one has ever said wisdom requires poverty. A philosopher can own great wealth. But it must not be wealth torn from others or stained with blood. It must be earned without wronging anyone and without using shameful methods. It must be gained honorably and spent honorably. It should be wealth that only spite itself could criticize. Make it as large as you want — it will still be honorable if it includes much that everyone would want to own, but nothing that anyone can claim was stolen from them. Such a man will not lose Fortune's favor. He won't boast about his inheritance, but he won't be ashamed of it either, if it was earned honorably. Yet he will have something to boast about if he throws open his house, lets all his fellow citizens walk among his possessions, and says: "If anyone recognizes something here that belongs to him, let him take it." What a great man! How excellently rich he will be if, after saying this, he still owns everything he had before! So I say that if he can safely and confidently let the people examine his accounts, and no one can find anything they can claim, such a man can boldly and openly enjoy his wealth.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: The wise man will not allow a single ill-won penny to cross his threshold: yet he will not refuse or close his door against great riches, if they are the gift of fortune and the product of virtue: what reason has he for grudging them good quarters: let them come and be his guests: he will neither brag of them nor hide them away: the one is the part of a silly, the other of a cowardly and paltry spirit, which, as it were, muffles up a good thing in its lap. Neither will he, as I said before, turn them out of his house: for what will he say? will he say, "You are useless," or "I do not know how to use riches?" As he is capable of performing a journey upon his own feet, but yet would prefer to mount a carriage, just so he will be capable of being poor, yet will wish to be rich; he will own wealth, but will view it as an uncertain possession which will some day fly away from him.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: The wise man won't let a single dishonestly earned penny into his house. But he won't refuse great wealth if it comes from good fortune and virtue. Why should he resent good things? Let them come and be his guests. He won't brag about them or hide them away. Bragging is foolish. Hiding them is cowardly and petty — like wrapping something good in your lap where no one can see it. He won't kick them out of his house either. What would he say? "You're useless" or "I don't know how to use money"? He can walk on his own feet, but he'd still prefer to ride in a carriage. He can handle being poor, but he'd rather be rich. He'll own wealth, but he'll see it as something uncertain that will fly away from him someday.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: He will not allow it to be a burden either to himself or to any one else: he will give it—why do you prick up your ears? why do you open your pockets?—he will give it either to good men or to those whom it may make into good men. He will give it after having taken the utmost pains to choose those who are fittest to receive it, as becomes one who bears in mind that he ought to give an account of what he spends as well as of what he receives. He will give for good and commendable reasons, for a gift ill bestowed counts as a shameful loss: he will have an easily opened pocket, but not one with a hole in it, so that much may be taken out of it, yet nothing may fall out of it.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: He won't let his wealth become a burden to himself or anyone else. He will give it away—why are you perking up? Why are you reaching for your wallet?—he will give it to good people or to those it might help become good. He will take great care to choose the most deserving recipients. After all, he knows he should account for what he spends just as much as what he earns. He will give for worthy and noble reasons, because a bad gift is as shameful as a loss. His pocket will open easily, but it won't have holes in it. Plenty can be taken out, but nothing will fall through by accident.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random. I do this man a service, I requite a good turn done me by that one: I help this other, because I pity him: this man, again, I teach to be no fit object for poverty to hold down or degrade. I shall not give some men anything, although they are in want, because, even if I do give to them they will still be in want: I shall proffer my bounty to some, and shall forcibly thrust it upon others: I cannot be neglecting my own interests while I am doing this: at no time do I make more people in my debt than when I am giving things away. "What?" say you, "do you give that you may receive again?" At any rate I do not give that I may throw my bounty away: what I give should be so placed that although I cannot ask for its return, yet it may be given back to me. A benefit should be invested in the same manner as a treasure buried deep in the earth, which you would not dig up unless actually obliged.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: Anyone who thinks giving is easy is wrong. It's actually very hard if you want to give wisely instead of just throwing money around randomly. I help this person because he deserves it. I pay back that person because he helped me first. I give to someone else because I feel sorry for him. And I teach another person skills so poverty can't crush him anymore. Some people I won't give anything to, even though they need help. Why? Because even if I give them money, they'll still be poor. With some people, I'll offer my help. With others, I'll force it on them whether they want it or not. While I'm doing all this, I can't ignore my own needs. I'm never more in people's debt than when I'm giving things away. "What?" you say. "You give so people will give back to you?" Well, I don't give just to waste my money. What I give should be placed where I can't demand it back, but it might come back to me anyway. Think of a good deed like treasure buried deep underground. You wouldn't dig it up unless you absolutely had to.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: Why, what opportunities of conferring benefits the mere house of a rich man affords? for who considers generous behaviour due only to those who wear the toga? Nature bids me do good to mankind—what difference does it make whether they be slaves or freemen, free-born or emancipated, whether their freedom be legally acquired or betowed by arrangement among friends? Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a benefit: consequently, money may be distributed even within one's own threshold, and a field may be found there for the practice of freehandedness, which is not so called because it is our duty towards free men, but because it takes its rise in a free-born mind. In the case of the wise man, this never falls upon base and unworthy recipients, and never becomes so exhausted as not, whenever it finds a worthy object, to flow as if its store was undiminished.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: Think about it — even a rich person's house is full of chances to help people. Who says you can only be generous to citizens? Nature tells me to do good for all people. What does it matter if they're slaves or free, born free or freed later? What does it matter how they got their freedom — legally or through some private deal between friends? Wherever you find a human being, you find a chance to help them. You can give money right at your own doorstep. You can practice generosity in your own home. And generosity isn't called that because it's only for free people — it's called that because it comes from a free spirit. For the wise person, this generosity never goes to worthless people. And it never runs dry. When it finds someone who deserves help, it flows as if the supply was endless.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: You have, therefore, no grounds for misunderstanding the honourable, brave, and spirited language which you hear from those who are studying wisdom: and first of all observe this, that a student of wisdom is not the same thing as a man who has made himself perfect in wisdom. The former will say to you, "In my talk I express the most admirable sentiments, yet I am still weltering amid countless ills. You must not force me to act up to my rules: at the present time I am forming myself, moulding my character, and striving to rise myself to the height of a great example. If I should ever succeed in carrying out all that I have set myself to accomplish, you may then demand that my words and deeds should correspond,"
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: So you have no reason to misunderstand the noble, brave, and passionate words you hear from people studying philosophy. But first, notice this important difference: someone learning wisdom is not the same as someone who has already perfected it. The student will tell you, "I talk about wonderful ideas, but I'm still drowning in countless problems. Don't expect me to live up to everything I say just yet. Right now I'm still working on myself, shaping my character, trying to reach the level of great role models. If I ever manage to do everything I've set out to do, then you can demand that my actions match my words."

happy-life_section-24.originalText: But he who has reached the summit of human perfection will deal otherwise with you, and will say, "In the first place, you have no business to allow yourself to sit in judgment upon your betters:" I have already obtained one proof of my righteousness in having become an object of dislike to bad men: however, to make you a rational answer, which I grudge to no man, listen to what I declare, and at what price I value all things. Riches, I say, are not a good thing; for if they were, they would make men good: now since that which is found even among bad men cannot be termed good, I do not allow them to be called so: nevertheless I admit that they are desirable and useful and contribute great comforts to our lives.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: But someone who has reached the peak of human excellence will handle you differently. He'll say: "First off, you have no right to judge people who are better than you. I already have proof that I'm on the right path — bad people hate me. But I'll give you a fair answer, which I don't mind doing for anyone. Listen to what I believe and how I value things. I say riches are not truly good. If they were, they would make people good. But since you find wealth even among bad people, it can't be called good. Still, I admit that riches are useful and desirable. They bring real comfort to our lives."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge[5] and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge. Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: So let's figure this out. We both agree these things are worth having. But let me explain why I don't count them as truly good things, and how I'd act differently than you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Surround me with gold and silver dishes used for everyday meals. I won't think I'm a better person because of these things. Even though they're in my house, they're not part of who I am. Now drag me away to the wooden bridge and dump me there with the beggars. I won't look down on myself because I'm sitting with people who hold out their hands for money. What does it matter if you lack a piece of bread when you still have the power to die? So what's my point? I'd rather have the magnificent house than sit on the beggar's bridge. Put me among beautiful furniture and every luxury you can imagine. I won't think I'm any happier just because my cloak is soft or because my guests recline on purple cushions.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Let me paint you a different picture: I won't be more miserable if my tired head has to rest on a bundle of hay instead of a soft pillow. I won't suffer more if I have to lie on some torn circus cushion with stuffing poking through the holes. So what's my point? Sure, I'd rather appear in public wearing fine wool and official robes than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like my daily business to go exactly as I want it to. I'd love to have one success follow another. But I won't let myself become proud of this good fortune. Now flip it all around — let losses and grief and all kinds of attacks tear at my spirit. Let every hour bring some new argument or problem. Even surrounded by the worst miseries, I still won't call myself the most wretched person alive. I won't curse any particular day. Why? Because I've made sure I don't have unlucky days.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows. The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive. I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than struggle to overcome my sorrows. The great Socrates would agree with me. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations. Let me ride in Bacchus's golden chariot from sunrise to Thebes. Let Persian kings take laws from me. Even when everyone salutes me as a god, I'll still know I'm just a man. Then connect this peak to a sudden fall into disaster. Put me on a foreign chariot to decorate some cruel conqueror's victory parade. I'll follow behind another's chariot with no more shame than I showed standing in my own. So what then? Despite all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the captive. I despise Fortune's entire realm, but if I had to choose, I'd pick the better parts. I'll turn whatever happens to me into something good — but I'd prefer what happens to be comfortable, pleasant, and unlikely to irritate me. Don't think any virtue comes without effort. Some virtues need the spur, others need the reins."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill. Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight. This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Think about walking. Sometimes you have to hold yourself back going downhill. Sometimes you have to push yourself hard going uphill. Virtues work the same way. Some virtues are uphill climbs — patience, courage, staying strong when life hits you hard. These virtues have to fight against tough opposition and crush bad luck under their feet. They're climbing, struggling, fighting their way up a steep hill. But other virtues are downhill walks — being generous, moderate, gentle. These flow easily. With the downhill virtues, you have to hold back your spirit so it doesn't run away from you. With the uphill virtues, you have to push and drive yourself forward. So we should use the tough, fighting virtues when we're poor. And we should use the lighter, more careful virtues when we're rich — the ones that move easily and just carry their own weight. Given this difference, I'd rather deal with virtues I can practice in peace than ones I can only test through blood and sweat. "That's why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. You just don't understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words. You don't try to figure out what they actually mean."

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: "What's the difference between me as a fool and you as a wise man?" The difference is everything. For a wise man, riches are servants. For a fool, riches are masters. You get used to wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise man thinks most about poverty when he's surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. War may never come, but it's always possible. You get arrogant about your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Riches go to your head, as if they were safe from all danger and so vast that Fortune herself couldn't swallow them whole.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: You sit there playing with your money, blind to the dangers ahead. You're like those primitive tribes under siege. They don't understand siege weapons, so they just watch the enemy build their war machines in the distance. They have no idea what's coming. That's exactly what you're doing. You sleep soundly on your pile of wealth, never thinking about all the disasters waiting to strike from every direction. Soon they'll strip you of everything valuable. But if you take riches away from a wise person, they still have everything that truly belongs to them. They live happily in the present and feel no fear about the future.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.'" This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them:
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: The great Socrates, or anyone else with that same strength to resist life's pressures, would say: 'I have one firm rule — I won't change how I live just to please you. Go ahead and criticize me from every angle with your usual complaints. I won't think you're attacking me. You're just crying like babies.' This is what a wise person says. Their mind is free from flaws, so they can call out others — not because they hate them, but because they want to help them improve.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able. I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: And he will add, "Your opinion hurts me — not for my sake, but for yours. When you hate what is good and attack virtue, you are giving up all hope of doing well yourself. You do me no harm. People don't hurt the gods when they tear down their altars. But it's clear you have evil intentions and would do harm if you could. I put up with your empty talk the same way Jupiter puts up with the silly stories poets tell about him. One poet gives him wings, another gives him horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him being cruel to the gods or unfair to people. Another makes him a seducer who kidnaps noble young men by force — even his own relatives. Another calls him a father-killer who stole someone else's kingdom from his own father."

happy-life_section-26.originalText: The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions. But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: The only result of such stories is that people feel less ashamed of their sins. They think it's okay because the gods supposedly do the same things. This doesn't hurt me personally, but for your own good, I urge you: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed her for years. They shout that what they follow is powerful — and grows more powerful every day. Honor virtue as you would honor the gods. Honor her followers as you would honor priests. And when sacred writings are mentioned, _favete linguis_ — give us your silence. This phrase doesn't come from the word 'favor' like most people think. It commands silence so that sacred rituals can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence. Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired.
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: It's much more important that you be told to do this: whenever that oracle speaks, you should listen carefully and quietly. But look what actually happens. Someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it. Someone cuts their arms and shoulders with shallow wounds, making themselves bleed, and pretends to be holy. Someone crawls down the street on their knees, howling. An old man in linen robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that some god is angry. And what do you do? You gather around these people and hang on their every word. You feed off each other's amazement, all agreeing that these frauds must be divinely inspired.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: Behold! from that prison of his, which by entering he cleansed from shame and rendered more honourable than any senate house, Socrates addresses you, saying: "What is this madness of yours? what is this disposition, at war alike with gods and men, which leads you to calumniate virtue and to outrage holiness with malicious accusations? Praise good men, if you are able: if not, pass them by in silence: if indeed you take pleasure in this offensive abusiveness, fall foul of one another: for when you rave against Heaven, I do not say that you commit sacrilege, but you waste your time.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: Look! From his prison cell — which he made more honorable than any senate house just by being there — Socrates speaks to you: "What's wrong with you? Why are you at war with both gods and men? Why do you slander virtue and attack holy things with nasty lies? If you can praise good people, then do it. If you can't, just stay quiet. If you really enjoy being this offensive and abusive, then attack each other instead. When you rage against Heaven, I won't say you're committing sacrilege — but you're wasting your time."

happy-life_section-27.originalText: I once afforded Aristophanes with the subject of a jest: since then all the crew of comic poets have made me a mark for their envenomed wit: my virtue has been made to shine more brightly by the very blows which have been aimed at it, for it is to its advantage to be brought before the public and exposed to temptation, nor do any people understand its greatness more than those who by their assaults have made trial of its strength. The hardness of flint is known to none so well as to those who strike it. I offer myself to all attacks, like some lonely rock in a shallow sea, which the waves never cease to beat upon from whatever quarter they may come, but which they cannot thereby move from its place nor yet wear away, for however many years they may unceasingly dash against it. Bound upon me, rush upon me, I will overcome you by enduring your onset: whatever strikes against that which is firm and unconquerable merely injures itself by its own violence. Wherefore, seek some soft and yielding object to pierce with your darts.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: I once gave Aristophanes material for a joke. Ever since, all the comic poets have made me their target for poisonous humor. Their attacks have only made my virtue shine brighter. Virtue benefits from being tested in public and exposed to temptation. No one understands how strong virtue is better than those who attack it and test its strength. No one knows how hard flint is better than those who strike it. I stand ready for all attacks, like a lone rock in shallow water. Waves beat against it constantly from every direction, but they can't move it or wear it down, no matter how many years they pound against it. Come at me, rush at me — I will defeat you by enduring whatever you throw at me. When something strikes what is solid and unbreakable, it only hurts itself with its own force. So go find something soft to pierce with your arrows.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: But have you leisure to peer into other men's evil deeds and to sit in judgment upon anybody? to ask how it is that this philosopher has so roomy a house, or that one so good a dinner? Do you look at other people's pimples while you yourselves are covered with countless ulcers? This is as though one who was eaten up by the mange were to point with scorn at the moles and warts on the bodies of the handsomest men. Reproach Plato with having sought for money, reproach Aristotle with having obtained it, Democritus with having disregarded it, Epicurus with having spent it: cast Phaedrus and Alcibiades in my own teeth, you who reach the height of enjoyment whenever you get an opportunity of imitating our vices! Why do you not rather cast your eyes around yourselves at the ills which tear you to pieces on every side, some attacking you from without, some burning in your own bosoms? However little you know your own place, mankind has not yet come to such a pass that you can have leisure to wag your tongues to the reproach of your betters.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: But do you really have time to dig into other people's bad behavior and judge them? To ask why this philosopher has such a big house, or why that one eats so well? You're looking at other people's pimples while you're covered with countless sores. It's like someone eaten alive by disease pointing and mocking the moles and warts on beautiful people. Go ahead — criticize Plato for wanting money, Aristotle for getting it, Democritus for ignoring it, Epicurus for spending it. Throw my own friends in my face, you who get your biggest thrill from copying our worst habits! Why don't you look around at your own problems instead? They're tearing you apart from every direction — some attacking from outside, some burning inside your own heart. You clearly don't know your place in this world. But humanity hasn't fallen so low that you can afford to waste time bad-mouthing your betters.

happy-life_section-28.originalText:
This you do not understand, and you bear a countenance which
does not befit your condition, like many men who sit in the circus
or the theatre without having learned that their home is already
in mourning: but I, looking forward from a lofty standpoint, can
see what storms are either threatening you, and will burst in
torrents upon you somewhat later, or are close upon you and on the
point of sweeping away all that you possess. Why, though you are
hardly aware of it, is there not a whirling hurricane at this moment
spinning round and confusing your minds, making them seek and avoid
the very same things, now raising them aloft and now dashing them
below? . . . . . .”
happy-life_section-28.plainEnglish: You don't understand this. You wear an expression that doesn't match your real situation. You're like people who sit in the circus or theater, not knowing their house is already burning down. But I can see from up high what storms are coming for you. They will either hit you later like a flood, or they're already close and about to sweep away everything you own. Even though you barely notice it, isn't there a spinning hurricane right now confusing your mind? It makes you chase after things, then run from the same things. It lifts you up one moment, then crashes you down the next.
